title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether integrating a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier plus a bounded automated repair budget increases the fraction of intent‑driven network‑change proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator. Each paired intent produced one shared_initial generation reused for both conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (deterministic validation and ≤1 automated repair). Outcomes: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.9966667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under the supplied synthetic suite and a single‑repair budget the single‑shot generator was near ceiling, limiting observable deterministic rescue. We archive preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts and interpret results with respect to estimand conditioning, validator coverage, repair budget, and operational deployment policies.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. For pre‑deployment network changes, semantic correctness—sequencing constraints, reachability, and policy preservation—is operationally critical and not captured by superficial syntactic checks alone. A widely proposed engineering pattern is a generate→validate→repair scaffold in which a deterministic verifier guards a generative proposal and a bounded repair operator attempts correction before human escalation. The measurable benefit of such guarded pipelines depends on the experimental estimand (what is held fixed), the generator single‑shot quality, the validator's expressiveness, and the permitted repair budget. Many prior evaluations conflate verifier benefits with benefits from additional model draws or verifier‑guided regeneration; isolating the deterministic rescue attributable to post‑generation checking alone is important for operational policies that limit model calls [1–4].

We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) that conditions on a single LLM draw per intent (the shared_initial estimand). For each intent the pipeline produced exactly one shared_initial candidate (gpt-5-mini) which was evaluated under two treatments: (a) baseline — accept the single candidate without repair; (b) guarded — run a deterministic validator and allow at most one automated repair followed by re‑validation. The primary research question: does adding a deterministic verifier plus at most one automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation compared with accepting that same candidate without repair? Our contributions are (i) a preregistered paired evaluation isolating deterministic rescue under shared_initial conditioning, (ii) a complete archived execution and analysis bundle supporting the reported results, and (iii) an evidence‑grounded interpretation of ceiling effects, validator coverage, and operational tradeoffs for NetOps CI/CD pipelines.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and system papers document rapid progress in LLM‑assisted NetOps and intent translation, and they emphasize the diversity of system scaffolds and the sensitivity of outcomes to validator and tooling design [1–4]. Tool‑augmented and planner‑centric frameworks enable LLMs to call external validators, simulators, and synthesizers to decompose multi‑step NetOps workflows [5,6]. Empirical work shows that deterministic checks and generate→validate→repair scaffolds can improve correctness metrics relative to unconstrained generation, but reported magnitudes depend heavily on validator coverage, task distribution, and whether pipelines permit resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration [3,4].

Two methodological themes motivated our design. First, prior evaluations often mix gains from deterministic validation with gains from multiple independent model draws or verifier‑guided regeneration; that conflation makes it hard to bound the deterministic rescue attributable to post‑generation checking alone [3]. Second, many NetOps benchmarks emphasize syntactic or template correctness rather than semantically rich invariants (sequencing, reachability, policy preservation), complicating operational interpretation [2,7]. Our work follows calls in the literature for clearer estimand definition and for evaluations tied explicitly to validator semantics and permitted repair budgets [3,5].
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The full confirmatory design was preregistered (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) before observing main outcomes. The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded − baseline) on N = 300 pairs after the preregistered inclusion/exclusion rules. The confirmatory analysis executor and multiplicity handling were fixed in the preregistration. The preregistration also specified a pilot (n = 60) for discordance estimation; that pilot was not executed.

Task suite and stratification. Tasks were produced deterministically by a registered task generator into a synthetic topology suite stratified into three difficulty strata (low/medium/high). Each task encodes: (i) natural‑language intent; (ii) initial and expected final device states; (iii) sequencing constraints (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields); (iv) preserve_unspecified_state invariants; and (v) protected_interfaces. Difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count) defined stratum membership; the main run sampled 100 pairs per stratum for the confirmatory N = 300.

Shared_initial protocol and model configuration. To isolate deterministic verifier/repair effects from resampling, the shared_initial estimand was enforced: for each pair a single shared_initial candidate was generated (requested model: gpt-5-mini) and reused verbatim by both baseline and guarded conditions. This ensures any difference arises only from deterministic validation and bounded repair applied to an identical generator output, mirroring operational policies that constrain model calls for latency, cost, or governance reasons.

Validator, scoring rule, and repair operator. Semantic evaluation used a deterministic validator implementing a full_intent_constraint_validation rule that checks sequencing invariants, required command counts, preservation of unspecified state, topology reachability invariants encoded by the synthetic suite, and forbidden‑template protections for protected_interfaces. Scoring was binary: an unflagged candidate counts as a pass. The guarded pipeline permitted at most one automated repair per pair (repair budget ≤ 1). The repair operator was a constrained edit routine limited to localized sequencing and insertion edits (for example, inserting a missing 'admin down' before a VLAN or MTU change). Repairs were applied only when the validator flagged the shared_initial candidate and were deterministically re‑validated; any candidate still flagged after the permitted edits counted as a failure for the guarded condition in the primary analysis.

Contamination controls and missingness handling. The preregistration included deterministic contamination detection (negative controls and invariant checks) and explicit exclusion rules: a pair would be excluded from confirmatory analysis only if both pipeline calls failed due to provider/infrastructure outage. If only one call failed, the pair would be retained per the executor's complete_pair_primary rule; sensitivity analyses treat single‑call failures as failures. All provider/API failures and exclusions were logged.

Execution auditing and reproducibility. The run used a hosted NetOps adapter in a scientific confirmatory mode that enforced the shared_initial protocol and repair budget. Execution and analysis artifacts (task manifests, model responses, validator traces, repair traces, and analysis inputs) were archived to permit deterministic replay of the confirmatory executor. Readers may consult the archived run bundle associated with the preregistered study id for full low‑level provenance and machine‑readable manifests.
sections.results:
Execution integrity and accounting. The preregistered adapter completed the confirmatory run: completed_episode_count = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions), complete_pair_count = 300, and model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared_initial generations plus one repair invocation). Deterministic reconciliation confirmed consistent episode accounting and no dual‑call provider outages.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Binary scoring produced baseline_success_count = 299 and guarded_success_count = 300, i.e., baseline = 299/300 (0.9966667) and guarded = 300/300 (1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The exact two‑sided McNemar test (operating on n10 and n01) returned p = 1.0. The absolute paired improvement (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0033333. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval computed with seed = 1729 and B = 10000 is [0.00, 0.01]. Because discordance is minimal (m = n10 + n01 = 1), the exact test has limited sensitivity and the bootstrap CI bounds the plausible absolute improvement to at most one percentage point in this experimental context.

Per‑stratum diagnostics and repair trace. Per stratum counts were: low baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; medium baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; high baseline = 99/100 and guarded = 100/100. Thus the single discordant case occurred in the high difficulty stratum. That episode invoked the permitted automated repair: the validator flagged a sequencing omission (missing explicit shutdown before a VLAN/MTU change), the constrained repair inserted the missing sequencing command, and the validator thereafter reported a pass. The solitary deterministic rescue therefore required one additional repair stage call and no iterative resampling.

Contamination and missingness. Contamination checks reported no unexpected pass behavior for negative controls. The missingness summary reports zero failed or unscorable episodes and zero excluded pairs under the preregistered rules.

Operational cost metric. The guarded pipeline produced one deterministic rescue at the cost of a single additional repair invocation across 300 pairs (model_calls_used = 301), indicating a low marginal model‑call footprint for bounded deterministic repair under this synthetic suite and edit operator design.
sections.discussion:
Estimand conditioning and operational alignment. Conditioning on a single shared_initial LLM draw aligns with policies that strictly limit model calls. Under this estimand the guarded pipeline measures only deterministic validator/repair rescue applied to an identical generator output; it does not capture benefits available from resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration, which represent different operational choices and estimands. Evaluations that permit resampling should use an alternative preregistered design since they measure cumulative generator variance exploitation rather than bounded post‑hoc correction.

Ceiling effects and pilot omission. The preregistration targeted detection of a 10 percentage‑point absolute improvement with planned power ≈0.8 conditioned on pilot‑estimated discordance. Because the optional calibration pilot was not executed, the main run confronted a near‑ceiling baseline (299/300), producing minimal discordance and limited inferential sensitivity to small absolute effects. This outcome illustrates the practical value of small calibration pilots when generator performance may approach ceiling on the chosen task suite.

Validator coverage and failure‑mode dependence. The single observed failure was a sequencing omission; other failure classes (reachability violations, forbidden ACL removal) were not observed at scale on this synthetic suite. The guarded pipeline's marginal utility will therefore depend on (i) the true deployment distribution of failure modes and (ii) validator expressiveness: validators that detect richer reachability or ACL semantics can increase observable rescue rates. Conversely, operator policies that forbid automated edits reduce the guarded pipeline to a detection‑and‑escalation mechanism rather than an automatic rescue tool.

Repair budget tradeoffs. We intentionally limited automated repair to a single constrained edit to measure bounded deterministic rescue. Iterative repair, larger edit operators, or interactive verifier‑guided generation would increase rescue opportunities but address a different estimand and impose higher model‑call or orchestration costs. The archived single episode repair trace provides an empirical data point for designing permissible edit sets and for estimating marginal cost per deterministic rescue under bounded budgets.

Implications for NetOps CI/CD. Organizations must align evaluation estimands with deployment policies. If pipelines permit multiple model calls and verifier‑guided regeneration, evaluations should allow resampling to estimate achievable success rates under those choices. If model calls are tightly budgeted, the shared_initial estimand provides a conservative operationally meaningful bound on verifier/repair rescue applied to a single candidate.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired comparison between a verifier‑assisted pipeline (deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair) and accepting a single‑shot LLM candidate under the shared_initial estimand on 300 synthetic NetOps intents using gpt-5-mini. Baseline single‑shot generation produced 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.00333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01]). Deterministic validator+repair rescued one sequencing omission under the bounded repair budget. The near‑ceiling baseline limits inferential sensitivity in this experimental context. Full preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts are archived to enable targeted follow‑up studies that vary estimand conditioning, model strength, task distribution, or repair budget.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were generated by the registered deterministic task generator; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase verifier marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were evaluated; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements relative to larger pre‑specified targets.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (resampling or iterative generation).
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
